summary: Defines a MIB with the elements common to monitoring any network service application. It is a standards-track document at the proposed standard level.

plainLanguage.summary: Whatever service you run, this gives one common dashboard for basic facts such as is it up.

questions: how to monitor a network service with snmp
what is the network services monitoring mib
how do i monitor a mail server with snmp
subtitle: A common SNMP table that lets one tool see whether any network service is up and who is connected to it.

tldr.problem: Plenty of tools watch low-level network gear, but few watch application-level network services such as mail transfer agents and directory service agents. Watching them only through lower-layer information is neither efficient nor reasonable.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2788 defines a read-only SNMP MIB module with an application table (one row per monitorable service) and an association table (one row per active connection), covering status, counters and timestamps.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2248. It deliberately stays minimal, so each kind of service is expected to add its own MIB on top of it.

today: RFC 2788 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2000. It obsoletes RFC 2248, and the metadata for this RFC lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Monitor Applications
sections.content:
The RFC starts from a gap: much effort has gone into managing lower-layer network facilities, but relatively little into managing application layer entities. Managing them using only lower-layer information gets harder as the applications get more complex.

The motivating examples are distributed components such as Message Transfer Agents (MTAs) and Directory Service Agents (DSAs). Reasons to monitor them include measuring load, detecting broken connectivity, isolating system failures and locating congestion.

Two requirements follow: it must be possible to monitor a large number of components, and application monitoring must be integrated into general network management. The RFC provides simple read-only access, which is enough to learn up or down status and to hint at a broad class of operational problems.
sections.plainLanguage: Checking only the roads does not tell you whether a shop at the end is open. You have to ask the shop itself.

sections.title: What Is In and Out of Scope
sections.content:
This MIB covers only what is common to monitoring any network service application. It does not give everything needed to monitor one specific application. Each type of service is expected to have a MIB of its own that builds on these common facilities. The MTA and DSA MIBs are the two examples the introduction names.

The RFC lists things it leaves out: configuration monitoring and control, examining or changing entries in service-specific request queues, probing the status of one specific request, and asking for actions to be performed. Such features would need strict security checking and a much more complex design, so the document says it "religiously keeps things simple".

It also does not manage the host the service runs on, nor applications that provide something other than a network service. For those, it points to the Host Resources MIB and the application MIB.
sections.plainLanguage: It is only the front-door sign. It does not let you rearrange the shop or look inside the cash register.

sections.title: The Application Table
sections.content:
The core is applTable, which has one row for each operational network service application on the system. Rows are indexed by an integer applIndex (1 to 2147483647). The only static information held about the application is its name. The RFC says other static information should come from directory services.

The link to those directories is applDirectoryName, a Distinguished Name that relates the SNMP entry to the X.500 Directory; an empty string means no directory information is available. applURL and applDescription can point to or briefly describe the application in a status display, and the RFC notes that actual configuration details may be kept elsewhere.

Each row also carries applVersion and applUptime, plus applLastChange, the time the application entered its current state. Timestamps hold sysUpTime values, or zero if the event happened before the network management subsystem last started.
sections.plainLanguage: The table is a list with one line per service. Each line says its name, where to read more about it, and when it last changed.

sections.title: Status and Association Counters
sections.content:
applOperStatus reports the state of the service as one of six values: up, down, halted, congested, restarting or quiescing. The last one means the service is operational but shutting down, and it may reject further inbound associations.

An association is a connection between two applications. An inbound association is one where this application is the responder; an outbound one is where it is the initiator. The table holds current counts of each (applInboundAssociations, applOutboundAssociations, as gauges) and running totals since initialization (applAccumulatedInboundAssociations, applAccumulatedOutboundAssociations, as counters), along with the time of the last inbound and outbound activity.

Two more counters track trouble. applRejectedInboundAssociations counts inbound associations the application rejected itself, and applFailedOutboundAssociations counts outbound attempts that failed. Neither is included in the accumulated totals. The RFC warns the rejected count may not reflect the true number of failures, since it ignores rejections at lower layers.
sections.plainLanguage: The sign shows open, closed or about to close, how many visitors are inside, how many came in total, and how many were turned away.

sections.title: The Association Table
sections.content:
The optional assocTable adds one row for each active association, indexed by applIndex and assocIndex. It tells you who is on the other end and what they are doing.

  • assocRemoteApplication: the name of the remote system, which for an IP-based application should be a domain name or IP address.
  • assocApplicationProtocol: an object identifier for the protocol. For Internet applications it has the form {applTCPProtoID port} or {applUDPProtoID port}, where the port is the primary port of the protocol. The RFC's example is SMTP as {applTCPProtoID 25}, assuming no other OID has been assigned.
  • assocApplicationType: uainitiator, uaresponder, peerinitiator or peerresponder, saying whether the remote side is a client or a peer and who started the connection.
  • assocDuration: the sysUpTime when the association started.
sections.plainLanguage: This is the visitor log: who is inside, which door they used and how long ago they arrived.

sections.title: Conformance and Changes from RFC 2248
sections.content:
The module defines compliance statements for three generations of the MIB (RFC 1565, RFC 2248 and RFC 2788). Those for RFC 1565 are marked obsolete and those for RFC 2248 are marked deprecated. The current ones are applRFC2788Compliance, which requires the application group, and assocRFC2788Compliance, which also requires the association group. That split is what makes association monitoring optional.

Compared with RFC 2248, this revision corrects a few minor technical errors, including the missing applDirectoryName in the conformance group. It changes applName, applVersion and applDescription from DisplayStrings to SnmpAdminStrings, and updates the distinguished-name reference from RFC 1779 to RFC 2253, which allows UTF-8.
sections.plainLanguage: There are checklists saying how much of the sign a service must show. The new version fixes mistakes in the older checklist.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
No object in this MIB has a MAX-ACCESS of read-write or read-create. If it is implemented correctly, an intruder cannot change or create its objects using SNMP SET operations.

The data can still be sensitive. It reveals the existence, type and configuration of applications on a host, which could hint at a vulnerability, and the network-usage information could be used to analyze traffic patterns.

SNMPv1 by itself is not a secure environment, even on a secure network such as one using IPSec. The RFC recommends the SNMPv3 framework, specifically the User-based Security Model (RFC 2574) and the View-based Access Control Model (RFC 2575). It is then up to the user to configure the SNMP entity so only legitimate principals can reach the objects.
sections.plainLanguage: Nobody can change the sign, but a stranger who can read it learns a lot about the shop, so only the right people should be allowed to look.

items.label: down
items.desc: The network service is not available.

items.label: congested
items.desc: Operational but no additional inbound associations can be accommodated.

items.label: restarting
items.desc: Currently unavailable, restarting, and will be available soon.

items.label: quiescing
items.desc: Operational but shutting down; new inbound associations may be rejected.
